articles.title: Brickbat: Penalty for Posting
articles.content:
Four police officers woke and arrested Will Fraser, a 15-year-old Reform U.K. activist, at his Walsall home. More than two months later, police still have not clearly explained the exact reason for the arrest, but The Telegraph found that it stems from a few Facebook posts. For example, Fraser criticized a Tory member of the Wolverhampton City Council for wearing casual clothes at meetings, then later remarked that he was glad the councilor was "not looking like a rent boy." Officers took Fraser to the station, questioned him, took his DNA and fingerprints, seized his phone and laptop, and released him on bail while banning him from council meetings. His lawyers and free speech groups say the arrest was an overreaction that threatens free speech, while the councilor in question claims the posts felt like targeted harassment.

The post Brickbat: Penalty for Posting appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Second Amendment Roundup: "Sensitive Places" Issue Coming to a Head?
articles.content:
Dr. Angus McClellan has just posted 151 pages of "Additional Research on Comprehensive Security and Sensitive Places" showing that at the Founding armed security was tied to each of Bruen's three sensitive places where arms could be restricted. Historical tradition from the American colonies and early states demonstrates that the predicate for banning weapons by the public at courts, legislative assemblies, and polling places was the government's provision of real protection in fact. That research supplements Dr. McClellan's compendium "The Second Amendment, Sensitive Places, and Comprehensive Government Security" which I summarized here.
In Wolford, the Supreme Court found Hawaii's law banning firearms on private property open to the public without affirmative consent of the owner – aka, the "Vampire Rule" – to violate the Second Amendment. The Court took notice of, but did not resolve, the issue that, "On a large portion of the land within the State's boundaries, possession of a firearm is now flatly prohibited." That issue has been pending in the several states that sought to nullify Bruen's holding that firearm carry permits may not be restricted to a privileged few or denied for purported lack of "need." One of those states is New Jersey, and early this year the Third Circuit en banc held oral argument about that ban in Koons v. Attorney General. See my post here.
The premise of these bans is that any place is "sensitive" if the legislature so declares. While it is often argued that being crowded suffices, that is belied by the fact that the bans include vast acreage of wooded parklands inhabited primarily by deer and squirrels. But Bruen explicitly rejected an arms prohibition based on being crowded, explicitly mentioning Manhattan as an example. Bruen did not go into the factual historical tradition justifying gun bans in the three locations it mentioned, as the issue was not before the Court. And that's where the research by Dr. McClellan fills the gap.
As prefaced in his "Additional Research," McClellan states: "The primary purpose of this additional research is to determine whether all 13 original colonies or early states had armed, government security personnel assigned to doorways at the sensitive places of courthouses/courtrooms, legislative buildings/chambers, and polling places." A secondary purpose, he continues, is to confirm that courthouses, legislatures, and polling places were indeed "sensitive," i.e., governments could or did ban weapons there. As for the method of research: "There are four sought-after elements in the historical material for determining whether a place had comprehensive security: a government agent was assigned to the place; his duties included maintaining security; he guarded a doorway; he carried a weapon." Finally, a "sensitive place" was "one where arms were prohibited." The research compiles sources showing where bans were enacted with evidence that such places were secured.
McClellan's research is truly overwhelming and is supported by hundreds of footnotes. Weapons were not necessarily always banned in the subject places, but they could be; the ultimate point is that these places were secured by government agents. I will mention only one entry illustrative of each of the identified sensitive places.
Courthouses. At the trial of Aaron Burr, General James Wilkinson was disarmed in the court by the U.S. marshal to prevent him from intimidating the jury, indicating at least that (1) weapons were or could be banned in court, (2) government officers were present in court to disarm people. Wilkinson was a senior U.S. Army officer who had conspired with Burr to raise an army to seize Spanish territory. He turned against Burr and served then as the prosecutor's chief witness. At the grand jury proceeding, the jury foreman was John Randolph of Roanoke, who upon seeing Wilkinson with a sword, alerted the marshal (1807).
Legislative assemblies. The Philadelphia Convention was off-limits to civilians entirely. Armed sentinels guarded the doorway to the hall, both inside and out. Note also that "it was standard procedure for legislative bodies to meet in secret" (1787).
Polling places. Delaware: Sheriffs shall be judges of elections, and he and other officers shall be required to preserve good order and keep the peace. Inspectors shall, when taking the [voice] votes or tickets, call out loud the name of the elector, and shall then place the tickets into a ballot box (1772).
The pattern was consistent: where the government required citizens to disarm, it supplied the protection itself. At other times, the government required citizens to arm themselves, such as in colonial times when going to church.
"Sensitive places" was never meant to be a blank check. At the Third Circuit's en banc argument in Koons, Judge Paul Matey asked New Jersey counsel whether courts should "really be overreading Heller's colorful use of the phrase 'sensitive places' as actually creating a doctrine," likening it to "large capacity magazines or assault weapons" — "a regulatory term that could be applied to anything that a regulator wants to regulate and then used as a claim for historical justification."
The one principle that does come from history is government-provided security. As Judge Matey put it: "at least one example of what it means could be places where government provided comprehensive security, right. And so we would know that that courthouse, a military base, these are places where … going armed was severely restricted. I mean, isn't that a helpful way of thinking about this?" The State's reply was that "the history is just not there." The record says otherwise.
Without a security limiting principle, there is neither security nor a principle. The Fourth Circuit in Kipke v. Moore upheld Maryland's gun bans on transit, parks, hospitals, museums, stadiums, and casinos on "crowded" and "vulnerable" theories — the very rationales Bruen rejected for Manhattan. Judge Agee, dissenting, called the sensitive-places exception "narrow" and warned that the majority had turned it into a license.
Comprehensive security makes sense. If the government takes no steps to prevent armed aggressors from entering a place, calling it a "sensitive" location is meaningless and reckless joke. Exercise of the Second Amendment right then remains the constitutionally-mandated default.
The post Second Amendment Roundup: "Sensitive Places" Issue Coming to a Head? appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Eleventh Circuit Rejects Netchoice's Challenge to Georgia Law Restricting Under-16-Year-Old Social Media Access
articles.content:
From today's Eleventh Circuit opinion in Netchoice v. Attorney General, by Judge Kevin Newsom, joined by Judges Robert Luck and Gerald Bard Tjoflat:
The State of Georgia recently enacted SB 351 to restrict minors' ability to create accounts on social-media platforms. The law requires platforms within its ambit to verify the ages of all their users, to prohibit minors under the age of 16 from creating accounts without their parents' consent, and to limit the personal data they use to display ads to users under 16.
The court held that Netchoice hadn't introduced enough evidence to show the law was facially unconstitutional:
Even in First Amendment cases, where the facial-challenge bar is lower than it otherwise might be, the plaintiff [in a facial challenge] must show that "a substantial number of [the law's] applications are unconstitutional, judged in relation to the statute's plainly legitimate sweep." Netchoice v. Moody …
To discharge its facial-challenge burden, NetChoice must provide the reviewing court with the data—either hard facts or, at the very least, sufficient briefing—necessary to conduct the Moody-required comparative analysis. It hasn't done so here. Indeed, NetChoice hasn't provided even a full list of its own members to which SB 351 applies. Instead, it has provided only an exemplary few: SB 351, NetChoice says, "regulates some websites operated by NetChoice members, including: (1) Dreamwidth; (2) Meta (Facebook and Instagram); (3) Nextdoor; (4) Pinterest; (5) Reddit; (6) Snap Inc. (Snapchat); (7) X; and (8) YouTube," as well as "new members … such as Tumblr." And though NetChoice contends that, in addition to its own members, SB 351 regulates "other covered 'social media' websites," it doesn't name any that (in whole or in part) host unprotected speech. In that respect, we think, NetChoice makes the same mistake that it made before in Moody: treating the law as having "certain heartland applications" and "mostly confin[ing its] battle to that terrain."
We've learned the facial-challenge lesson the hard way. In Moody, the Supreme Court, even while largely agreeing with our merits analysis, faulted us for "mostly confin[ing] [our] analysis" to "certain heartland applications" instead of "address[ing] the full range of activities the law[ ] cover[ed]." The Court went on to observe that even if it were to attempt the facial analysis itself, it couldn't "undertake the needed inquiries" because the "parties ha[d] not briefed the critical issues [t]here, and the record [wa]s underdeveloped." The Court therefore vacated and remanded our case … "to consider the scope of the laws' applications, and weigh the unconstitutional as against the constitutional ones." In turn, … we … remanded [the case] to the district court[] for further development of the issues pertinent to the facial-challenge analysis.
We are similarly stymied here. For the foregoing reasons, we conclude that NetChoice has failed to satisfy Moody because it hasn't adequately addressed the "full range" of SB 351's applications, and the record before us does not permit the weighing Moody requires.
The court also rejected Netchoice's vagueness challenge:
The district court held, and NetChoice contends before us, that SB 351's requirement that social-media platforms use "commercially reasonable" age-verification mechanisms renders the statute unconstitutionally vague.
The problem, as NetChoice candidly acknowledges, is that "the district court raised this issue sua sponte." … In granting injunctive relief on a theory that NetChoice never pleaded, the district court erred. See Clark v. Sweeney (2025) (holding that courts "transgress[ ] the party-presentation principle" when "granting relief on a claim that [the plaintiff] never asserted and that [the defendant] never had the chance to address").
And the court rejected Netchoice's 47 U.S.C. § 230 objection to the advertising restrictions:
Section 230 prohibits treating a social-media platform as "the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider." … [But] SB 351's advertising provision doesn't treat social-media platforms as publishers or speakers of information provided by others. Rather, it regulates how social-media platforms themselves act by forbidding them from targeting minors with ads based on personal information. This type of regulation falls outside § 230's ambit, which preempts laws that seek to hold social-media platforms "liable for information originating with a third-party user."
John Henry Thompson, Christopher Michael Carr, Riley B. Liu, Elijah J. O'Kelley, and Logan B. Winkles of the Georgia AG's office represent the state.
The post Eleventh Circuit Rejects Netchoice's Challenge to Georgia Law Restricting Under-16-Year-Old Social Media Access appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Why Some Americans Living Abroad Would Rather Renounce Their Citizenship Than File Taxes
articles.content:
For many Americans overseas, the scariest day this month is not Halloween, but October 15—the final extended deadline for filing income tax returns with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS).
An estimated 3.3 million U.S. citizens live abroad, although the number is likely an undercount because the government doesn't keep a comprehensive list or require Americans overseas to register their residence. Still, American citizens and resident aliens living abroad must pay U.S. income taxes and comply with domestic tax filing requirements, regardless of where they live or work. They must also complete the dizzying process of reporting any foreign bank accounts, assets, and financial interests in foreign institutions.
When filing their income tax returns, most Americans living abroad have zero tax liability. In its 2025 Annual Report to Congress, the Taxpayer Advocate Service—an independent organization within the IRS that helps people navigate tax problems—found that for Americans overseas, "the percent of individual international tax returns reporting no tax liability is significantly higher than domestic taxpayers." Yet, the agency reports that the filing process is "complex, overlapping, and punitive." The report says failure to comply results in "harsh and disproportionate penalties…even when taxpayers make good-faith mistakes or owe no U.S. tax."
The U.S. income tax rate is low compared to other high-income countries, so Americans living overseas typically pay more in local taxes than they would here. Still, Brandon Mitchener, executive director at Tax Fairness for Americans Abroad, tells Reason that Americans living outside the U.S. are often oblivious to their income tax obligations, assuming they're exempt because they already pay taxes in their country of residence. He says that complex U.S. tax laws and financial regulations force many Americans living overseas to request an extension to October 15.
The date also coincides with the final deadline for the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) and the Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR)—regulations that require Americans with foreign financial assets above a certain threshold to declare the value of their assets to the IRS or Treasury Department.
Under FATCA, Americans living overseas with foreign financial assets exceeding $200,000 at year-end or more than $300,000 at any point during the year must declare their assets when filing their income tax return. The law also requires foreign financial institutions to report information about U.S. account holders directly to the IRS. Originally enacted to catch Americans overseas engaged in tax evasion or other criminal financial activity, it has instead made American citizenship an impediment for expatriates looking to save or invest money outside the U.S.
"Because of FATCA, many foreign financial institutions shun American clients," Mitchener says. This includes Trade Republic, a German digital bank and online brokerage firm that doesn't accept U.S. citizens living abroad, a category of people it tellingly describes as "FATCA customers."
"Some charge a premium for banking-while-American," he adds, while some have "even de-banked American clients." The latter is a very real concern for Madison Berry, an American living in the Netherlands. She tells Reason she's "a little bit worried" that her European bank will one day "come back and be like, 'Oh, you're a U.S. citizen. We're gonna close your account.'"
This "reduces choice and raises the cost and complexity of everyday financial products for Americans abroad, from basic savings accounts to mortgages and retirement savings," Mitchener says, creating problems unique to America and Eritrea, the only two countries that tax citizens living outside their borders.
Compounding matters, Americans with foreign financial accounts exceeding $10,000 must file an FBAR with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, even though the form duplicates much of the same information already reported through FATCA. The reporting requirements make investing or saving money abroad prohibitive for Americans and foreign financial institutions, with foreign banks opting to close existing accounts or outright denying Americans the opportunity to open a bank account, according to a 2019 report by the Government Accountability Office. Seven years later, little has changed. The IRS itself admits that its systems and functions are "inaccessible to or incompatible with the needs of taxpayers living abroad, creating unnecessary barriers to compliance."
Berry says figuring out her tax obligations and reporting requirements has left her "in a financial limbo." "I seriously considered renouncing my U.S. citizenship as part of the process just to make life easier." She's not alone.
Several Americans living overseas who spoke to Reason on condition of anonymity said they were also considering renouncing their U.S. citizenship rather than deal with the onerous annual tax filing process. One American living in Ireland who owns and operates a U.S.-based business says she uses a remote desktop and virtual private network to access her financial institutions to avoid scrutiny.
Another tells Reason she's considering renouncing her citizenship because America's tax system is "predatory in how complicated it is and how much responsibility it puts on ordinary people to figure everything out themselves."
The post Why Some Americans Living Abroad Would Rather Renounce Their Citizenship Than File Taxes appeared first on Reason Magazine.
